title: Car on a circular track
stem: A car travels at a constant speed of 20 m/s around a flat circular track of radius 50 m. What is the car's acceleration?

correct.text: 8.0 m/s² directed toward the center of the track
correct.rationale: The velocity direction changes continuously, so there is an acceleration of magnitude v²/r = (20 m/s)²/(50 m) = 8.0 m/s², directed toward the center.

wrong.text: 0 m/s², because the speed is constant
wrong.rationale: Constant speed does not mean zero acceleration. The velocity vector keeps changing direction, which requires the inward acceleration v²/r = 8.0 m/s².
wrong.error_pattern: equates constant speed with zero acceleration

wrong.text: 0.40 m/s² directed toward the center of the track
wrong.rationale: This divides the speed by the radius (v/r) instead of using v²/r. The correct magnitude is (20)²/50 = 8.0 m/s².
wrong.error_pattern: uses v/r instead of v²/r

wrong.text: 8.0 m/s² directed away from the center of the track
wrong.rationale: The magnitude v²/r = 8.0 m/s² is right, but the acceleration of a body in uniform circular motion points inward, toward the center, not outward.
wrong.error_pattern: outward (centrifugal) direction for the acceleration

change_note: New context (car on a flat track) with numbers; same uniform-circular-motion acceleration idea; distractors are zero-acceleration, v/r and outward-direction errors.

title: Ball on a string, speed doubled
stem: A ball on a light string moves at constant speed in a horizontal circle of fixed radius on a frictionless table, and the string tension is the only horizontal force on the ball. The ball is then set moving at twice the original speed in a circle of the same radius. How does the string tension compare with its original value?

correct.rationale: The tension is the net force, which supplies the centripetal acceleration: T = mv²/r. With r fixed, doubling v multiplies the tension by 2² = 4.

wrong.rationale: This treats the required inward force as proportional to v. Because T = mv²/r, it is proportional to v², so doubling the speed gives a factor of 4, not 2.
wrong.error_pattern: treats centripetal force as proportional to v rather than v²

wrong.text: It is unchanged, because the speed is still constant
wrong.rationale: Constant speed does not mean no net force. The ball always accelerates inward at v²/r, and a larger v requires a larger inward force, so the tension increases.
wrong.error_pattern: equates constant speed with unchanged or zero net force

wrong.rationale: This inverts the dependence on speed. The required inward force grows as v², so doubling the speed increases the tension by a factor of 4.
wrong.error_pattern: inverts the v² dependence

change_note: Conceptual proportional reasoning about a=v²/r and F=mv²/r with doubled speed; new context (ball on string).

title: Hammer-throw ball
stem: In a hammer throw, a 4.0 kg ball moves in a horizontal circle of radius 1.5 m with a constant period of 0.50 s. Neglect gravity's effect on the circle. What is the magnitude of the net force on the ball?

correct.rationale: The speed is v = 2πr/T ≈ 18.8 m/s. The net force is the centripetal force F = mv²/r = (4.0)(18.8)²/1.5 ≈ 950 N, directed inward.

wrong.rationale: This is mv, the product of mass and speed, which is not a force. The centripetal force needs v²/r: mv²/r ≈ 950 N.
wrong.error_pattern: uses mv instead of mv²/r

wrong.rationale: This uses 4π²r/T instead of 4π²r/T², leaving the period unsquared. With a = 4π²r/T² the net force is 4.0 × 4π² × 1.5/0.25 ≈ 950 N.
wrong.error_pattern: forgets to square the period

wrong.rationale: This multiplies mv² by the radius (mv²r ≈ 2132 N) instead of dividing by it. The centripetal force is mv²/r ≈ 950 N.
wrong.error_pattern: multiplies by r instead of dividing

change_note: Multi-step: v=2πr/T then F=mv²/r with new numbers; same uniform-circular-motion acceleration/net-force concept.

title: Work by a quadratic force
stem: A variable force F(x) = 3.0x² (F in newtons, x in meters) acts on a crate along the x-axis. How much work does this force do on the crate from x = 1.0 m to x = 3.0 m?

wrong.rationale: This multiplies the final force F(3.0) = 27 N by the full 2.0 m displacement. The force is not constant, so the work must be the integral, which is 26 J.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the final force as if constant over the displacement

wrong.rationale: This averages the force at the two endpoints, (3 + 27)/2, and multiplies by 2.0 m. That shortcut is exact only for a force that is linear in x; F = 3x² is not, so the integral gives 26 J.
wrong.error_pattern: endpoint-average shortcut for a nonlinear force

wrong.rationale: This evaluates the antiderivative x³ only at the upper limit and forgets to subtract its value at the lower limit (1). The definite integral is 27 − 1 = 26 J.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the lower-limit term of the definite integral

change_note: New force function and limits; same W = ∫F(x)dx idea; distractors mirror the seed's constant-force and endpoint-average errors plus a dropped lower limit.

title: Work by a force that reverses sign
stem: A force F(x) = 8.0 − 2.0x (F in newtons, x in meters) acts on an object along the x-axis. How much net work does it do as the object moves from x = 0 to x = 6.0 m?

correct.rationale: W = ∫(8.0 − 2.0x) dx from 0 to 6.0 = [8.0x − x²] = 48 − 36 = 12 J. The force reverses at x = 4.0 m, so part of the path contributes negative work.

wrong.rationale: This stops at x = 4.0 m, where the force becomes zero, and ignores the region from 4.0 m to 6.0 m. The force there points opposite to the motion and does −4 J of work, so the net work is 12 J.
wrong.error_pattern: ignores the negative-work region

wrong.rationale: This adds the magnitudes of the two areas (16 J + 4 J). Work done where the force opposes the motion is negative and must be subtracted, giving 16 − 4 = 12 J.
wrong.error_pattern: adds areas without regard to sign

wrong.rationale: This multiplies the final force F(6.0) = −4.0 N by the full 6.0 m. The force changes along the path, so the work is the integral, 12 J.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the final force as if constant over the displacement

change_note: Linear force that changes sign; signed-area integral; new numbers and function.

title: Work by an exponentially decaying force
stem: A force F(x) = 20e^(−0.50x) (F in newtons, x in meters) acts on an object along the x-axis. How much work does it do from x = 0 to x = 2.0 m?

wrong.rationale: This multiplies the final force F(2.0) = 20e^(−1) ≈ 7.36 N by the 2.0 m displacement. The force decays along the path, so the work is the integral, about 25.3 J.
wrong.error_pattern: uses the final force as if constant over the displacement

wrong.rationale: This integrates without dividing by the coefficient 0.50 in the exponent: 20(1 − e^(−1)) ≈ 12.6 J. The antiderivative of e^(−0.50x) is −2.0e^(−0.50x), so the correct result is twice as large.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the chain-rule factor when integrating the exponential

wrong.rationale: This averages the endpoint forces, (20 + 7.36)/2, and multiplies by 2.0 m. For a nonlinear force that over-estimates the integral, which is about 25.3 J.
wrong.error_pattern: endpoint-average shortcut for a nonlinear force

change_note: Exponential force with chain-rule factor; same W = ∫F(x)dx idea; hardest of the three.

title: Force from a quartic potential
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with potential energy U(x) = bx⁴, where b is a positive constant. The x-component of the force on the particle is

correct.rationale: The force is the negative derivative of the potential energy: F = −dU/dx = −4bx³.

wrong.rationale: This lowers the power correctly but forgets the power-rule factor of 4 that comes down when differentiating x⁴.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the power-rule factor

wrong.rationale: This brings down the factor 4 but leaves the exponent unchanged. Differentiating x⁴ gives x³.
wrong.error_pattern: wrong exponent after differentiating

wrong.rationale: This integrates U(x) instead of differentiating it. The force is the negative derivative of U, not its antiderivative.
wrong.error_pattern: integrates instead of differentiating

change_note: New potential (quartic) and symbolic constant; same F = −dU/dx; no sign-only distractor in this variant.

title: Force at a point from a cubic potential
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with potential energy U(x) = 3.0x² − 2.0x³ (U in joules, x in meters). What is the x-component of the force on the particle at x = 2.0 m?

wrong.rationale: This is dU/dx, the slope of U, without the minus sign. The force is the negative of the slope, so F = +12 N.
wrong.error_pattern: omits the minus sign in F = −dU/dx

wrong.rationale: This is the value of U at x = 2.0 m (12 − 16 = −4.0 J) reported as a force. The force comes from the derivative of U, not from U itself.
wrong.error_pattern: reports the potential energy value instead of its derivative

wrong.rationale: This differentiates the cubic term as 3x², dropping its coefficient 2.0, giving 6.0x − 3.0x² = 0 at x = 2.0 m. The correct derivative of 2.0x³ is 6.0x², so F = +12 N.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the coefficient when differentiating the cubic term

change_note: Numeric evaluation of F = −dU/dx at a point; this is the one variant of the seed with a sign-only distractor.

title: Force from an inverse-square potential
stem: A particle moves along the positive x-axis with potential energy U(x) = 4.0/x² (U in joules, x in meters). What is the force on the particle at x = 0.50 m?

correct.rationale: F = −dU/dx = −d(4.0x⁻²)/dx = +8.0x⁻³ = 8.0/(0.50)³ = 64 N. The positive sign means the force pushes the particle toward larger x, where U is lower.

wrong.rationale: This forgets the power-rule factor of 2 from x⁻², giving 4.0/x³. Differentiating 4.0x⁻² gives 8.0x⁻³, so the force is 64 N.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the power-rule factor

wrong.rationale: This is the value of U at x = 0.50 m (4.0/0.25 = 16 J) used as a force. The force is the negative derivative of U, not U itself.
wrong.error_pattern: reports the potential energy value instead of its derivative

wrong.rationale: This brings down the factor 2 but leaves the exponent as −4 (8.0/x⁴). Differentiating x⁻² lowers the exponent to −3, so the force is 8.0/x³ = 64 N.
wrong.error_pattern: wrong exponent after differentiating

change_note: Negative power of x, so exponent and sign handling are harder; same F = −dU/dx idea.

title: Block at the end of its oscillation
stem: A block on a frictionless horizontal spring oscillates with amplitude 0.20 m. At the instant the block reaches x = +0.20 m, the end of its motion, which statement is correct?

correct.text: Its speed is zero and its potential energy equals the total energy
correct.rationale: At the end of its motion the block momentarily stops, so its kinetic energy is zero and all of the mechanical energy is spring potential energy: U = E.

wrong.text: Its speed is maximum and its potential energy is zero
wrong.rationale: That describes the equilibrium position x = 0. At x = +0.20 m the block is momentarily at rest and the spring potential energy is at its maximum, equal to the total energy.
wrong.error_pattern: confuses the turning point with the equilibrium position

wrong.text: The net force on it is zero
wrong.rationale: The spring force −kx has its largest magnitude at x = 0.20 m. The block is only momentarily at rest, and this force reverses its motion.
wrong.error_pattern: assumes zero speed means zero net force

wrong.text: Its kinetic energy equals its potential energy
wrong.rationale: The kinetic energy is zero here while the potential energy equals the total energy, which is not zero. The two are equal only at an intermediate position.
wrong.error_pattern: splits the energy evenly at the extreme

change_note: Spring-block turning point instead of a general potential; same K = 0, U = E idea.

title: Turning points in a parabolic well
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with potential energy U(x) = 2.0x² (U in joules, x in meters) and total mechanical energy 8.0 J. At which positions are its turning points?

correct.rationale: At a turning point the kinetic energy is zero, so U = E: 2.0x² = 8.0 gives x² = 4.0 and x = ±2.0 m.

wrong.rationale: This solves 2.0x = 8.0, treating U as linear in x. The potential energy is 2.0x², so x² = 4.0 and x = ±2.0 m.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the square when solving U(x) = E

wrong.rationale: This sets x² = 8.0, ignoring the factor 2.0 in U(x) = 2.0x² (or reading it as a spring constant in ½kx²). Solving 2.0x² = 8.0 gives x = ±2.0 m.
wrong.error_pattern: ignores the coefficient in U(x)

wrong.text: There are no turning points, because the force at x = ±2.0 m is not zero
wrong.rationale: A turning point does not require zero force. The force F = −4.0x is −8.0 N at x = +2.0 m, and it is this nonzero force that reverses the particle's motion there.
wrong.error_pattern: assumes force must be zero at a turning point

change_note: Numeric turning points from U(x) = E for a new potential and energy.

title: Allowed region in a double-well potential
stem: A particle moves along the x-axis with potential energy U(x) = 0.50(x² − 4.0)² (U in joules, x in meters). Its total mechanical energy is 4.5 J, and it is observed at x = +2.0 m. Within what range of positions is its motion confined?

correct.rationale: Motion is allowed only where K = E − U ≥ 0, that is U ≤ 4.5 J. This requires |x² − 4.0| ≤ 3.0, so 1.0 ≤ x² ≤ 7.0. The region around x = 0 has U > E and cannot be crossed, so a particle at x = +2.0 m stays between x = 1.00 m and x = 2.65 m.

wrong.rationale: This treats only the outer turning points as limits. Between x = −1.0 m and x = +1.0 m the potential energy exceeds 4.5 J (it is 8.0 J at x = 0), so the particle cannot cross that barrier.
wrong.error_pattern: ignores the inner turning points where U exceeds E

wrong.rationale: This reads the limits of x² (1.0 and 7.0) as limits of x. The turning points are the square roots, x = 1.00 m and x = 2.65 m.
wrong.error_pattern: reports x² values as positions

wrong.rationale: This treats the starting point x = 2.0 m as a turning point. There U = 0 and the kinetic energy is 4.5 J, the maximum, so the particle keeps moving to x = 2.65 m before turning around.
wrong.error_pattern: treats the observation point as a turning point

change_note: Non-monotonic potential: requires U <= E, barrier reasoning and the correct connected region; same turning-point idea.

title: Rope pulling a crate at an angle
stem: A rope pulls a crate with a constant force of 50 N directed 60° above the horizontal. The crate moves horizontally at a constant 4.0 m/s. What power does the rope's force deliver to the crate?

correct.rationale: Power is the dot product P = F·v = Fv cos θ = (50)(4.0)cos 60° = 100 W.

wrong.rationale: This is Fv with no angle. Only the component of the force parallel to the velocity delivers power, so the cosine factor is needed: 100 W.
wrong.error_pattern: ignores the angle between force and velocity

wrong.rationale: This uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°. The angle is measured from the horizontal motion, so the parallel component is F cos 60°, giving 100 W.
wrong.error_pattern: uses sine instead of cosine

wrong.rationale: This divides the parallel force component by the speed (25 N ÷ 4.0 m/s ≈ 6.3 W) instead of multiplying. Power is P = F·v = 25 N × 4.0 m/s = 100 W.
wrong.error_pattern: divides instead of multiplies

change_note: Numeric P = Fv cos θ with an angle between F and v; new context.

title: Power from a work function
stem: The total work done on a cart by the net force is W(t) = 2.0t³ joules, where t is in seconds. What is the instantaneous power delivered to the cart at t = 2.0 s?

correct.rationale: Instantaneous power is the time derivative of work: P = dW/dt = 6.0t². At t = 2.0 s, P = 6.0(4.0) = 24 W.

wrong.rationale: This is the average power over the first 2.0 s, W/t = 16 J/2.0 s. Instantaneous power is the derivative dW/dt, which is 24 W at this instant.
wrong.error_pattern: uses average power instead of the derivative

wrong.rationale: This is the work done so far, 16 J, reported as a power. Power is the rate of change of work, dW/dt = 24 W.
wrong.error_pattern: reports W instead of dW/dt

wrong.rationale: This differentiates 2.0t³ as 3t², dropping the coefficient 2.0. The derivative is 6.0t², giving 24 W.
wrong.error_pattern: drops the coefficient when differentiating

change_note: Calculus definition P = dW/dt of instantaneous power from a function; new context.

title: Power from a time-dependent force
stem: A 2.0 kg cart starts from rest on a frictionless track. A force along the track, F = 8.0t newtons (t in seconds), is the only horizontal force on it. What power does this force deliver at t = 1.5 s?

correct.rationale: a = F/m = 4.0t, so v = ∫a dt = 2.0t². At t = 1.5 s, v = 4.5 m/s and F = 12 N, so P = Fv = 54 W.

wrong.rationale: This uses the constant-acceleration formula v = at with the final acceleration (6.0 m/s²), giving v = 9.0 m/s. The acceleration grows with time, so v must be found by integrating: v = 4.5 m/s and P = 54 W.
wrong.error_pattern: applies constant-acceleration formulas when acceleration varies

wrong.rationale: This multiplies force by acceleration (12 N × 6.0 m/s²), which is not a rate of energy transfer. Power is F·v, with v = 4.5 m/s, giving 54 W.
wrong.error_pattern: uses F·a instead of F·v

wrong.rationale: This is the average power over the first 1.5 s: the work is ∫Fv dt = 4.0t⁴ = 20.25 J, and 20.25 J ÷ 1.5 s = 13.5 W. The question asks for the instantaneous power, 54 W.
wrong.error_pattern: uses average power instead of instantaneous power

change_note: Variable force: integrate a to get v, then P = F·v; distractors are constant-acceleration, F·a and average-power errors.
